objective_for_doctor: A 5-year-old Male patient presents to the clinic. Chief complaint: I have swelling in one or more areas of your body, swelling (right lateral side of the foot), and swelling (right top of the foot).

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?

Hi doctor. I have swelling on my feet—on the right side and top of my foot, and also on the left top and left sole. It hurts a little, about 3 out of 10, and the pain feels kind of sharp and heavy, starting pretty fast.

Doctor: I’ll ask a few quick questions to pinpoint this. Did the swelling start after a scrape/insect bite/plant thorn or any recent injury to the feet, and do you have fever or redness/warmth over the swollen areas?

No, I didn’t have a scrape, insect bite, or thorn that I remember, and I don’t think there was any recent injury. I’m not sure about fever, but the main thing is the swelling and pain; I don’t recall saying it’s very red or very warm.

Doctor: Any trouble walking or bearing weight, and is the swelling limited to the foot or is there swelling in the ankle/lower leg too? Also, have both feet swelled at the same time or one side first?

I have pain with the swelling, but I can still walk. The swelling is in the feet (right and left), not the ankle or lower leg that I noticed. It feels like it’s been on both sides around the same time.

Doctor: Thanks—any sores, blisters, or skin changes on the feet (especially between toes), and does anyone around you have similar swelling or a rash? Also, is the swelling coming and going with itch, or is it staying in the same spots?

No sores or blisters that I noticed, and no skin changes between the toes. I don’t know of anyone else with similar swelling or a rash. It seems to stay in the same spots rather than coming and going, and I don’t feel itch.

Doctor: I’m going to check a few things—do you see any pitting of the swelling when I press it with a finger, and can you tell me if the feet look pale or have color changes? Also, do you have pain mainly over a joint (like the ankle/foot joints) or more in the soft tissue, and are both feet the same degree of swelling?

I don’t know if it pits when you press it, but the swelling is there on both feet. I think the pain is more in the areas of swelling on the top and sides of the feet rather than one specific joint, and both feet look about the same swelling.

Doctor: I’ll check a few key details on exam—when I press the swollen areas, does it leave an indentation (pitting) or does it stay firm, and are the feet warmer than normal or is the skin normal-colored? Also, do you have any recent sore throat, stomach bug/diarrhea, or new medicines (including antibiotics) in the last 1–3 weeks?

REQUEST TEST: Urinalysis_and_Urine_Protein (dipstick + microscopy if available)  
REQUEST TEST: CBC_with_Differential  
REQUEST TEST: ESR_and_CRP  
REQUEST TEST: Serum_Albumin_and_Creatinine

I’m not sure if it leaves an indentation when you press it, and I don’t know about warmth compared to normal—I haven’t noticed the skin being unusually hot. I don’t remember having a sore throat or stomach bug/diarrhea recently, and I don’t know of any new medicines or antibiotics in the last couple weeks.

Doctor: I’m going to ask a couple last targeted questions: is the urine normal (no dark/foamy urine) and have you noticed swelling of the eyelids/face in the morning? Also, does the child have headaches, reduced energy, or high blood pressure readings if you’ve checked them?  
Doctor: If you can, we’ll also check one quick exam finding—does the swelling feel “spongy” (edema) versus hard, and are there any enlarged lymph nodes or a new rash?

I don’t know if my urine is dark or foamy. I haven’t noticed swelling of the eyelids/face in the morning. I also don’t have headaches or reduced energy that I can tell, and I don’t know about any blood pressure readings. The swelling feels kind of soft/spongy, and I haven’t noticed new rashes or swollen lymph nodes.

Doctor: Given the soft/spongy swelling in both feet, with no itch, no rash between toes, and uncertain pitting, I’m concerned about generalized fluid retention (edema). **REQUEST TEST: Urinalysis_and_Urine_Protein (dipstick + microscopy if available)**, **REQUEST TEST: CBC_with_Differential**, **REQUEST TEST: ESR_and_CRP**, and **REQUEST TEST: Serum_Albumin_and_Creatinine**—these help rule in/out kidney causes like nephrotic syndrome versus infection/inflammation.  

Doctor: Also, in the meantime, can you check whether the swelling is worse in the morning or late in the day, and whether the child has new abdominal pain, nausea, or foamy urine?
I think the swelling is about the same, not clearly worse in the morning or late in the day. I don’t have new abdominal pain or nausea that I can tell, and I don’t know about foamy urine.

Doctor: Thanks—so bilateral, relatively symmetric, soft/spongy foot edema without itch, rash, or clear warmth/redness, and with no known GI/URI symptoms. While we await the labs you mentioned (urinalysis/protein, CBC, ESR/CRP, albumin/creatinine), we’ll also check blood pressure and look for generalized edema signs like periorbital swelling. Are there any home/clinic BP readings yet, and did the child start the swelling within the last 1–7 days or has it been weeks?
I don’t have any home or clinic blood pressure readings yet. I think the swelling started recently—within the last week or so, not weeks.

Doctor: I’ll do a focused exam now—please have you check the child’s blood pressure and I’ll look for periorbital/facial swelling and any hidden edema elsewhere, and we’ll confirm whether the foot swelling pits with gentle finger pressure. Meanwhile, do you have the test results back from **urinalysis/urine protein, CBC, ESR/CRP, and serum albumin/creatinine** yet?  
REQUEST TEST: Basic_Metabolic_Panel (electrolytes, BUN/creatinine)  
REQUEST TEST: Blood_Pressure_Check (documented reading)
Doctor, I don’t have any blood pressure reading for you yet. And I don’t have the test results back for those urine/blood tests or the kidney/electrolyte tests you ordered.

Doctor: I’ll repeat the key “kidney screening” questions—does the child have foamy urine, dark urine, or any morning eyelid puffiness, and can you check and report the child’s weight change in the last week?  
Doctor: Also, please get a blood pressure reading today and, if possible, tell me the urine dipstick result for protein (positive/negative) so I can decide between nephrotic syndrome and other causes of bilateral foot edema.

I don’t know about foamy urine or dark urine, and I haven’t noticed morning eyelid puffiness. I don’t have the weight change numbers, but I have gained weight recently. I also don’t have the blood pressure reading or the urine dipstick protein result for you yet.

Doctor: I’m going to ask two final questions: does the child’s urine look normal in color/volume, and has the edema been strictly limited to the feet/soles without swelling of eyelids, hands, or abdomen? Also, can we urgently obtain a blood pressure reading and a urine dipstick for protein today (if you can)?  
Doctor: If those aren’t immediately available, I’ll treat this as likely nephrotic syndrome until proven otherwise and proceed with **REQUEST TEST: Urine_Dipstick_Protein_and_Specific_Gravity (STAT)** and **REQUEST TEST: Blood_Pressure_Check**; once results return, I’ll finalize the diagnosis.

My urine looks normal in color/volume as far as I can tell, and the swelling seems limited to the feet/soles—no eyelid, hand, or belly swelling that I’ve noticed. I can’t provide a urine dipstick protein result or a blood pressure number right now, but you can get those today.

Doctor: Thank you—because the swelling is bilateral, soft/spongy, and limited to the feet without rash/itch, I need the two key data points now: **REQUEST TEST: Urine_Dipstick_Protein_and_Specific_Gravity (STAT)** and **REQUEST TEST: Blood_Pressure_Check (today)**.  
Doctor: Once I have those results, I’ll decide if this is nephrotic syndrome (protein in urine ± normal-looking urine) versus another cause of bilateral edema, like inflammatory/systemic processes or less likely lymphatic/orthopedic issues.

Doctor, I can’t get or report the urine dipstick protein/specific gravity result right now, and I also don’t have the blood pressure reading today. Please do the urine dipstick and BP in clinic and I’ll answer any follow-up questions you have after you get the results.

Doctor: I’ll do a quick targeted assessment: can you confirm the swelling is truly symmetric on both feet and whether pressing the swollen areas creates a clear indentation (pitting) or leaves them unchanged, and do the soles/top feel warm compared with the rest of the skin?  
Doctor: While we’re in clinic, please proceed with **REQUEST TEST: Urine_Dipstick_Protein_and_Specific_Gravity (STAT)** and **REQUEST TEST: Blood_Pressure_Check (now)**, and I’ll base the diagnosis on those results given bilateral soft edema in a 5-year-old.

Yes, it seems symmetric on both feet. I’m not sure if pressing makes a clear indentation—maybe it doesn’t much—but it feels soft/spongy. I don’t think the soles or tops feel warmer than the rest of my skin.

Doctor: Thanks—so symmetric bilateral soft/spongy swelling with no clear warmth, no itch/rash, and (so far) no obvious facial/hand/abdominal edema makes me less confident about an acute infection and still most concerned about kidney-related edema, especially nephrotic syndrome, but I must confirm with urgent tests.  

Doctor: REQUEST TEST: Urine_Dipstick_Protein_and_Specific_Gravity (STAT) and REQUEST TEST: Blood_Pressure_Check (now).

Okay, doctor. Please do the urine dipstick (protein and specific gravity) and check my blood pressure now—those are the key things you need. I’ll wait for the results and answer any follow-up questions you have.

Doctor: I’m going to wait for the in-clinic **urine dipstick (protein + specific gravity)** and the **blood pressure** results; while we’re waiting, the key possibilities from your exam are nephrotic syndrome (often proteinuria) versus a less likely non-kidney cause of bilateral foot edema.  
Doctor: Once those results are back, I’ll finalize whether this is nephrotic syndrome or something else.
Yes, doctor. Please let me know the urine dipstick protein/specific gravity result and my blood pressure when you have them, and I’ll stay here for any next steps.

Doctor: I’m ready to decide, but I don’t yet have the two critical results you were asked for—your urine dipstick protein/specific gravity and your blood pressure—without them I can’t safely confirm the cause of the bilateral foot edema.  
Doctor: If the urine dipstick shows **significant protein** (or the albumin/creatinine is elevated) and blood pressure is normal, I’ll diagnose **nephrotic syndrome**; if blood pressure is high or urine shows blood/other concerning findings, it changes the diagnosis—so please obtain **urine dipstick protein/specific gravity STAT** and **blood pressure NOW** and tell me the numbers/results.

Doctor, I can’t provide the urine dipstick protein/specific gravity numbers or my blood pressure reading because I don’t have them in front of me right now. Please get those results and tell me the exact protein result (positive/negative and amount if you can) and the BP value, and I’ll answer anything else you need.

Doctor: I can’t finalize a safe diagnosis without the **urine dipstick protein/specific gravity** and a **blood pressure value**; please obtain both in clinic now and report the exact numbers/results to me.  
Doctor: While you do that, I’ll examine for periorbital edema and re-check for pitting edema on the shins/ankles, but the decision depends on urine protein and BP.  
Doctor: Once you provide those results, I’ll make a diagnosis immediately.

Doctor, I understand—but I don’t have the urine dipstick protein/specific gravity result or my blood pressure value right now to report to you. Please obtain them in clinic and tell me the exact numbers/results, and I’ll answer any follow-up questions immediately.

Doctor: I’m going to make a decision now based on what we have: a 5-year-old with **new, symmetric bilateral soft/spongy foot edema** without itch/rash or clear warmth/redness, and no reported facial/hand/abdominal swelling—this pattern most strongly suggests **nephrotic syndrome** until proven otherwise, even though we’re still missing the urine protein and BP numbers.  
DIAGNOSIS READY: Likely nephrotic syndrome (suspected), pending urine protein (dipstick/ACR) and blood pressure to confirm and assess severity/complications.
